rationale: The MIN operator is a genuinely conjunctive (non-linear) way to force both cheapness and cash-based earnings quality to bind, and the expression, hypothesis, and positive sign are mutually consistent — though the underlying ingredients (E/P and Sloan accruals) are canonical, so the only novelty on offer is the combination rule.

The hard indicator gate zeroes out roughly half the cross-section, so the short leg becomes "positive-accrual firms" regardless of EV yield and the signal largely degenerates into the accrual anomaly with a large mass point at zero destroying the ordering, on top of EBITDA/EV itself being a published value measure.

Internally consistent, but B/M multiplied by a smoothed low-accrual score is essentially the published value-plus-accounting-quality composite (Piotroski/QARP) and duplicates the mechanism of the first proposal with only a 3-period moving average distinguishing it.

Sign inconsistency: Compustat RECCH is the cash-flow-statement item "Accounts Receivable — Decrease (Increase)," so high RECCH/AT means receivables are *falling* (conservative), the opposite of the stated "accumulating receivables," and additionally the product's low tail is dominated by low sales-yield growth firms, so a negative expected sign implies going long expensive stocks.

The second gate (oancf > dvc) is satisfied by the overwhelming majority of dividend payers and is therefore nearly non-binding, so the signal reduces to dividend yield conditioned on negative accruals, and the multiplicative indicators pile non-payers and gate-failures into a single zero mass point that makes the short leg uninterpretable.

The expected sign contradicts the expression's natural direction — the signal is high for cheap firms (a positive predictor) and low for low/negative-E/P growth firms, so a negative expected sign implies a long leg of expensive stocks and requires the second-difference accrual term to overpower the value premium, which is implausible given both ranks are equally scaled.
